newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: CBOT Project A soybeans surge as resistance cracks.
newsitem.headline: CBOT Project A soybeans surge as resistance cracks.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) soybean futures soared on active U.S. fund buying on the exchange's after-hour Project A system, spurred by a breach of key upside technical resistance, traders said on Monday.
"It's not clear why the CBOT market gained so sharply in Asia today. But I think U.S. investment funds were active on technical buying," a trader at a major Tokyo commodity house said.
He said that some funds in North America had computer programs which generate buying automatically when prices reach certain levels.

The CBOT's May soybean contract was indicated at US$8.08 a bushel at 0830 GMT, up 14-3/4 cents from the close of open outcry trade in Chicago on Friday, but off a high of $8.13-1/2, while March was up 13 cents at $8.04.

A trader with South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said soybeans rallied on technical buying, after the May contract smashed though strong resistance at $8.00, which had held during Friday's open outcry session in Chicago.
The spark for the upward push appeared to be nervousness over weather reports from Brazil.

U.S. Weather Services Corporation reported at 0733 GMT on Monday thunderstorms and rainfall of 0.80-3.00 inches (20 mm) across the far north of Brazil, but so far only isolated showers of up to 0.20 inches (5.0 mm) in the central soybean growing state of Mato Grosso and the southern state of Parana.
The forecaster said the wet weather would slow harvests over northern locations, but was favourable for filling and maturing crops in the south.
"There is some panic buying of soybeans on Project A," one Taiwanese trader said. He speculated that weather conditions in Brazil might be behind the jump in futures.
"Heavy rain in Brazil's soybean growing areas could cause the price to surge," he said.
Rumours of industrial action at the key Brazilian soybean and soymeal exporting port of Paranagua were also contributing to the rally, but these could not be immediately confirmed.
There were delays in loading the harvest at Paranagua on Friday, but this was due to a lack of available trucks which has slowed the flow of new crop from the fields.

Ships face a wait of between 15 and 26 days in Paranagua, according to the trader questioned. On Friday, there were three vessels loading soybeans and soymeal at the port, while 17 were waiting to dock.

South Korean buyers are particularly nervous over the surge in futures prices as they are expected in the market soon for 80,000 tonnes of soymeal and have to buy around 80,000 tonnes of soybeans for oil processing for shipment in April.
